title: Salesforce vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Software Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Salesforce vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Software Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Robert Izquierdo, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 19, 2026 at 11:52 AM PST 6 min read
CRM
PLTR
BRZE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) represent two distinct ways to play the artificial intelligence boom. Which software provider offers the most compelling path for your portfolio over the next three years?

Salesforce provides a massive cloud platform for managing customer relationships, while Palantir builds operating systems that integrate disparate data for decision-making. Investors compare them because both are aggressively integrating generative AI into enterprise workflows to drive efficiency for global businesses.

The case for Salesforce

Salesforce provides customer relationship management (CRM) tools to businesses through its Agentforce 360 platform. The company is currently focused on deploying autonomous AI agents that can handle sales and service tasks without constant human oversight for its more than 10,000 customers. In its latest annual report, it also highlighted its expansive partner network and recent acquisitions like Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE) to bolster its data management and AI offerings.

In the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, revenue reached $43.9 billion, which is an 11.2% increase over the previous twelve-month period. Net income for this time frame was $9.7 billion, demonstrating the company's ability to maintain high profitability while transitioning to new AI products. This growth highlights the steady adoption of cloud-based tech stocks that focus on enterprise efficiency and customer retention.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, suggesting the company maintains a conservative level of borrowing relative to its equity. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to liabilities, was 0.8x. In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow reached $14.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 23.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Palantir Technologies

Palantir Technologies builds software platforms that allow organizations to integrate massive amounts of data with AI models for real-time decision-making. The company serves both government agencies and commercial enterprises, recently announcing a partnership with AmeriLife Group to apply AI in the insurance distribution market. Its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) is a core driver of its current strategy as more businesses look to move beyond simple chatbots toward operational AI tools.

Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) shares rose about 5% Thursday morning after U.S. prosecutors charged a Russian national with allegedly surveilling employees of a Silicon Valley technology company identified by Reuters as Palantir.

A federal grand jury indicted Igor D'iu on four counts, including conspiracy to act as a foreign government agent, interstate stalking and identification-document fraud. The Justice Department did not identify the company; Reuters cited two people familiar with the matter in naming Palantir.

title: Warren Buffett Says Berkshire Will Never Prefer Cash Over Good Businesses. History Says Your Portfolio Shouldn't Either.
detail:
Warren Buffett Says Berkshire Will Never Prefer Cash Over Good Businesses. History Says Your Portfolio Shouldn't Either.
Jack Delaney, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 19, 2026 at 10:50 AM PST 4 min read
BRK-B
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) has often been criticized for keeping too much cash on hand. As of Sept. 30, its cash pile, which includes rail and utility cash and Treasury bills, sat at $377.4 billion. For an idea of just how large that is, it's about the market cap of Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR).

That seems to conflict with the preferences of former CEO Warren Buffett, even when he was running the company. In a 2024 shareholder letter, he said, "Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned."

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

There's nuance in that statement, however, that offers insight into what investors should consider for their own portfolios.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

What history tells us about stock investing

The stock market is known for being one of the best sources of wealth creation. As a hypothetical example, a $100 investment at the start of 1928 in the S&P 500 would have been worth $1.1 million by the end of 2025 (dividends included). In comparison, a $100 investment in a three-month Treasury bill in 1928 that kept rolling into those bills was worth $2,578 at the end of 2025.

Based on those numbers alone, it seems less than ideal to keep such a large cash position on hand.

That said, going back to Buffett's quote, there was an important word: "prefer." Buffett is famous for seeking value, whether through acquisitions, stock purchases, or Berkshire's own share buybacks. He may have preferred investing in good businesses over cash and cash equivalents, but if he didn't find any, he was OK with keeping his money on the sidelines until he did.

Why keeping cash on the sidelines makes sense

How much money to keep outside the stock market is a question only an individual investor can answer best, as they know their investing goals and risk tolerance better than anyone. But having some cash to work with allows for more flexibility and will mean an investor isn't selling a position to free up money to pay for another, which can trigger tax implications.

For instance, in 2026, Berkshire's flexibility allowed it to acquire the homebuilder Taylor Morrison in a deal that represented a total enterprise value of $8.5 billion, purchase $10 billion worth of Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) stock in a private placement, and start a position in the Italian technology conglomerate Bending Spoons (NASDAQ:BSP), which just went public in July.

BigBear.ai Holdings, Inc. BBAI has witnessed a sharp selloff over the past month despite growing demand for its artificial intelligence (AI)-powered defense, intelligence and national security solutions. Concerns surrounding persistent losses, negative cash flows, shareholder dilution and uncertain profitability prospects have weighed on investor sentiment. Although BigBear.ai's expanding contract portfolio and improving revenue outlook offer long-term opportunities, near-term execution risks remain significant.

Over the past month, BigBear.ai shares have plunged 19.4%, underperforming the Zacks Computers - IT Services industry's 10.9% decline. The stock has also lagged the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's 12% decline and the S&P 500 Index's 5.5% fall.

BBAI's One-Month Price Performance

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The weakness comes despite BigBear.ai's third-quarter 2026 revenue growth of 31% year over year to $43.6 million. While improving business momentum and contract wins remain encouraging, the company's inability to generate sustainable profits continues to raise concerns about its investment appeal.

Persistent Losses Cloud BigBear.ai's Profit Outlook

BigBear.ai's widening losses remain a major concern. In the third quarter of 2026, the company reported a net loss of $91.9 million, or 19 cents per share, against a net income of $2.5 million in the year-ago period. The deterioration was primarily attributable to a $76.7 million noncash goodwill impairment charge.

Although adjusted EBITDA improved slightly to negative $9.1 million from negative $9.4 million a year earlier, the company remains unprofitable at the operating level. Selling, general and administrative expenses increased to $31.3 million from $25.3 million, reflecting higher labor costs, acquisition-related amortization and sales and marketing investments.

Research and development expenses also increased to $5.4 million from $3.4 million. These rising costs could continue to pressure profitability as BigBear.ai expands its AI offerings and customer base. Unless revenue growth translates into stronger operating leverage, the company's profitability concerns may persist.

Cash Burn and Dilution Risks Weigh on BBAI

BigBear.ai's negative operating cash flow presents another challenge. During the first nine months of 2026, net cash used in operating activities increased to $49.8 million from $20.1 million in the comparable year-ago period, highlighting continued pressure on cash generation.

Potential shareholder dilution also remains a concern. BigBear.ai's existing at-the-market equity offering arrangement allows additional share issuance, potentially reducing existing shareholders' ownership stakes. Its outstanding common shares increased to approximately 480.4 million at September 2026-end from 437 million at 2025-end.

Although the company maintained nearly $400 million in cash and investments at the end of the third quarter, sustained cash consumption could limit financial flexibility over time. Investors will likely seek evidence of improving cash conversion before becoming more confident about the company's financial sustainability.

title: Palantir just posted a record quarter—so why did the stock sink?

Palantir just posted a record quarter—so why did the stock sink?
Harry Jones

PLTR

NDX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing.com and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Investing.com — The Nasdaq-100 slid into correction territory at the start of November as investors questioned whether Big Tech's AI spending will pay off, putting high-multiple AI names under pressure. ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW), growing revenue at 21.8%, lost 30.0% in the month to November 17. Yet even Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR)—the AI software company behind the Gotham, Foundry, and AIP platforms, which just posted its fastest growth as a public company—has tumbled 15.8% over the past month to $156.56, including a 9.2% slide in the past week alone.

Palantir's sell-off is not a verdict on its business but the market repricing a stock that had already paid in advance for years of that growth. Analysts forecast revenue growth of 90.7% and EPS growth of 188.8%, figures that make every dip look like an entry point. Even after the pullback, though, Palantir trades at 102.8 times trailing earnings, a multiple that leaves no margin for a slower quarter.

Identifying when a software leader's valuation has outrun even record growth is what ProPicks AI is built for. In Tech Titans, InvestingPro's strategy dedicated to high-margin tech leaders, Palantir lost out to cash-generative tech names trading at far lower multiples—including a wireless chip designer, a specialty chip foundry, and a PC and printer maker.

See the cash-generative tech names Tech Titans holds instead: Explore the Tech Titans strategy on InvestingPro

The Software Customers Cannot Rip Out

Palantir makes its money by turning short AI pilots into large production contracts on platforms that customers find hard to replace. Gotham, Foundry, and AIP are built on a proprietary data ontology that wires the software into mission-critical workflows, creating high switching costs once a deployment goes live. AIP bootcamps have shortened the path from pilot to production—in the third quarter, one $1 million pilot converted into a $15 million annual contract value deal within the same quarter.

Third-quarter results showed that model at record scale. Revenue surged 96% year-over-year to $2.31 billion, the first quarter above $2 billion, and adjusted EPS of $0.44 topped the $0.41 consensus. U.S. commercial revenue climbed 148% to $984 million and overtook U.S. government revenue of $953 million for the first time in company history. Net dollar retention reached 165%, up 800 basis points from the prior quarter.

That growth converts into cash. GAAP net income reached $1.13 billion, a 49% margin, adjusted operating margin hit 62%, and adjusted free cash flow came in at $1.216 billion. Management raised full-year revenue guidance to $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion and adjusted free cash flow guidance to $4.8 billion to $5 billion, and the company holds $10.4 billion in cash and U.S. Treasury securities against just $225.3 million of total debt.

UiPath: Gradual Revenue Growth With Clear Seasonal Peaks

UiPath (NYSE:PATH) primarily generates revenue by delivering an integrated suite of enterprise software applications that empowers corporate entities, financial institutions, and government organizations to independently design, deploy, evaluate, and continuously manage automated business processes across their operations.

It recently reorganized its executive leadership team, formally appointing a new chief financial officer, and simultaneously introduced several advanced developer tools specifically designed to help large global enterprises dynamically map and orchestrate their various internal organizational workflows.
